title: Eighty years
hookLine: his body like an old cart kept going with straps (DN 16)

lines: THE OLD CAR THAT STILL GETS THERE.
cards: An old car someone in your family refused to give up. The door that only opens from the inside. The duct tape on the mirror.
It still gets there. Maybe you are that car some mornings. This week follows the Buddha's last journey, told in one long text, the Great Discourse on the Final Nibbana.
It's one of the most human texts in the whole canon. He's around eighty now, still walking from town to town, still teaching.
And during a rainy season near Vesali, he falls seriously ill, with sharp pains, close to death.

teach.h: HE HOLDS ON, TO SAY GOODBYE.
teach.b: The text says he bore the pain mindfully, without complaint. And he thought: it wouldn't be right for me to pass away without speaking to those who attended me, without taking leave of the community.
So, by strength of will, he pushed the illness back and held on to life. When he's recovered enough, he comes out and sits in the shade.
Ananda sits beside him and admits how frightened he was. When I saw you sick, my body went weak, he says. I couldn't think straight.
My only comfort was that you wouldn't go without leaving some instruction. Then the Buddha says something astonishingly frank about his own body. In paraphrase: I'm old now, Ananda.
Worn out. I've reached the end of my days. I'm turning eighty.

teach.h: LIKE AN OLD CART, HELD WITH STRAPS.
teach.b: Just as an old cart is kept going only by being held together with straps, the body of the one who has found the way is kept going only with that kind of help. A worn-out cart. Not a glowing god.
Not a body beyond aging. A man at eighty, held together with repairs. He adds that his body is only comfortable when he rests his mind in deep meditation, beyond all the signs of things.
Buddhist tradition holds that he had reached complete freedom.

teach.h: AWAKE, AND THE BODY STILL AGES.
teach.b: And the body still aged. It still hurt. Awakening didn't stop the cart from wearing out; what it changed was how he rode it.
The next pages have him still walking, still teaching, for months.

how: The Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the account of the Buddha's last journey, is read and studied across Buddhist traditions, and many Buddhists reflect on aging, sickness and death as natural parts of life, as he did.

o: his age when he called his body a worn-out cart
how many years the Buddha spent teaching
the age when monks may stop the alms round

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: near where he fell ill in the rains

s: the Buddha's body never aged or hurt after awakening
he called it a worn-out cart, held together with straps.
he held off his illness to take leave of the community
the text says he pushed it back by strength of will.
the story of his last journey is in one long text
the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the Great Discourse on the Final Nibbana.

games.q: you're eighty and gravely ill during the rainy season. your community hasn't heard your farewell. what do you do?
o: let go, and pass away quietly.
push the illness back, and hold on to say goodbye.
send word for a doctor from the city.
games.why: the text says he bore the pain mindfully and held on to life by will, because it wasn't right to go without taking leave.

practice: Slowly roll your shoulders, once, twice; tilt your head to one side, then the other; stretch your fingers wide, and let them close. Whatever aches, notice it without scolding.
Then silently thank this body, the whole worn, patched, faithful cart of it, for carrying you this far.

wordCard.voice: Eighty years. The Buddha at the end of his life, describing his own body as an old cart kept going with straps.

orig.note: Pali: old age, decay. One of the messengers that first sent Siddhartha out of the palace.

carryVoice: Your line: the old cart still rolls. Worn out, held with straps, and still on the road. That's day seventy-eight in the books.
